We stopped over at the late Barragán’s residence, right next door, where Mr. Romero was a docent when he was younger, so the place is, for him, a home away from home. For me it was a jaw-dropping sight. When you first walk into the entry hall you feel as if you’re staring up the stairs at a three-dimensional painting: every angle, every dimension, every shadow, every color and every light beam seems composed to alter and enhance your senses.
That whet my appetite for more visual treats, so we set off for some nearby galleries. First was the Galeria Labor, a tall, open space showing off “The Fractal Zoo,” a collection of large, angled steel poles joined by plastic heads by the French artist Etienne Chambaut, and then
Kurimanzutto,
a shed-like building infused with light from a long skylight, designed by another leading Mexican architect, Alberto Kalach.
We took our first break from this cultural marathon at the delightful Café Zena, a hole in the wall whose designers, a collaborative of architects called Tienda de Comercios, have outfitted a long alley with tables and chairs. At the end of this tunnel — just past the overhang of a sinuous staircase — is a large light well made of patterned cinder blocks. Over their coffee (excellent), Mr. Romero spoke again about the country’s upward trajectory, noting the new regime’s outlay of billions on security and infrastructure, but he was making the wrong pitch. He was leaving out that instead of a sprawling, impenetrable city, this one is full of charm, with a bit of sophistication amid beautiful, lush, walkable neighborhoods.
We finally made our way to Mr. Romero’s Museo Soumaya. The museum, in an emerging, formerly industrial area called New Polanco, was designed to reflect organic forms growing out of the earth, Mr. Romero said. It shocks you at first that a building can look like this. The torquing, windowless facade is clad with 16,000 hexagon-shaped aluminum panels, few of them alike and none of them touching. It’s one of those buildings that, love or hate it, you can’t stop looking at. There are so many variations of color, light and form that your eye never gets enough.
Inside, the highlight is the top floor, a circular space dominated by a giant skylight, from which projects an explosion of radiating structural beams. For a museum that’s emphatically contemporary, the art inside is surprisingly not so. The bulk is made up of European works from the 15th to 19th century. The heaving sculptures of one of these artists, Rodin, also helped inspire Romero’s contorted building form.
Our last stop was the most revelatory when it comes to Mexican design. The Museum of Anthropology, designed in 1963 by the Mexican architect Pedro Ramírez Vázquez, is just off the Paseo de la Reforma in the stately Polanco District. The building itself is hard to fathom — particularly its giant concrete canopy, which hovers above the main courtyard atop a single column. I’m not an engineer, and I have no idea how it stays up. And the collection inside is, simply, the finest record of Maya, Aztec, Oaxacan and more Mesoamerican civilizations. This includes wonderfully expressive art (I started to see where all of this intense form-making originated), ceramics, sculpture and, my favorite, the giant “Stone of the Sun,” an immense, elaborately carved stone circle that you suspect might start rolling away and then opening the earth.

The torch was passed the next day to Mr. Rojkind, whose pierced eyebrow and seriously scruffy hair suggested that he would be a very different guide from Mr. Romero. He is a literal rock star — the former drummer for the popular Mexican band Aleks Syntek y la Gente Normal; he still gets stopped on the street by fans.
And unlike my first tour guide, whose elite connections somewhat remove him from the local architecture scene, Mr. Rojkind lives to be part of it, eagerly teaming up with other designers and constantly promoting the city’s large collection of emerging architectural talent.
“When you see your parents fighting all the time, you don’t want to repeat that pattern,” he said of his generation’s propensity to work together.
Mr. Rojkind’s architecture strives not just to show off but also to transform the space around it, as we saw at our first stop, the Cineteca Nacional. Originally an aloof series of rough black plaster boxes in the scruffy Xoco neighborhood, Mr. Rojkind transformed it into a thriving campus. He removed a parking lot in front, making it the theaters’ main green. An aluminum canopy cut with triangular perforations provides shelter to this space and knits his new buildings together with the original ones. On the far side of his new construction Mr. Rojkind has built yet another park, this one designed for outdoor movies, projected onto a wall that’s meant to be a giant screen.
After this first stop, he directed me to one of the city’s great unknown architectural gems: the main campus of Mexico’s National Autonomous University, or UNAM, about 11 miles south of the historic center. The expansive campus, built in the 1950s, looks a bit worse for wear, but it is about as close as you can come to a museum of modernist architecture, warts and all. You stroll past examples of early Modernism, Streamline Moderne, Structural Expressionism, the International Style and much more, taking in sleek glass curtain walls, monumental facades, colorful building-size murals, gigantic arched roofs and zigzag-shaped structures. There are no tourists, just students and families, kicking soccer balls and eating street food.
And after a brief nearby sojourn into some more conventional tourism (a visit to Trotsky’s house — yes, he was assassinated in Mexico City; a walk through Coyoacan’s beautiful square and its many food stalls), I met Mr. Rojkind for drinks at the sushi restaurant he designed, Tori Tori, back in Polanco. The place looks like nothing from the street; there’s not even a sign. But when you walk through the door, you discover that Mr. Rojkind has covered the facade of an old house with two layers of diamond-patterned white steel. A patio outside the restaurant is walled in by a rain forest’s worth of vegetation and, inside, the highlight of the modern space is a small, Zen-like wood-clad room, with another lush green wall at its far end.
We then quickly stopped off for a smoky mezcal (or three) at the apartment of another celebrated Mexican architect, Enrique Norten, in the refined Condesa district, just southwest of Polanco. Of course you can’t visit his house, but you can take a trip to his new Chopo Museum in Cuauhtémoc, near the historic center, which we saw the next day. Mr. Norten installed a shimmering glass bar-shaped structure for exhibits in the upper reaches of a turn-of-the-century, wrought-iron building that was once moved here, piece by piece, from Germany. Just don’t go on a Monday or you’ll have to smooth talk your way in in broken Spanish, as we did.
We walked a few more blocks in a light rain to our final destination: the neighborhood taco joint, El Califa. It didn’t disappoint. Mr. Rojkind did all the ordering, and I still don’t know exactly what I ate, but I remember shoving every type of taco — pork? chicken? pineapple? — into my mouth and guzzling an amazing strawberry juice as the rowdy clientele cheered for the local soccer team, locked in a tie in the biggest match of the year. The goalie actually scored the winning goal, winning our ecstatic driver $500 in a bet. It was as unlikely an ending as there could be. About as unlikely as a weekend like this.

SECAUCUS, N.J. — In 1991, the Yankees selected Brien Taylor, a high school left-hander, with the first overall pick in baseball’s amateur draft. His failure to make the majors scared teams away from showing similar faith in a prep pitcher in the 22 drafts that followed.
That streak ended Thursday when the
Houston Astros
took Brady Aiken, a left-hander from Cathedral Catholic High School in San Diego, with the first pick in the 2014 draft.
To blame Taylor for the aversion to high school pitchers may seem unfair, but he stands out as perhaps the worst No. 1 pick since the draft was introduced in 1965. He not only never reached the major leagues but also never played above Class AA, with
an off-the-field fight in 1993
resulting in a badly injured rotator cuff. Taylor, Matt Bush (San Diego Padres, 2004) and Steve Chilcott (Mets, 1966) are the only No. 1 picks — aside from the last two, Mark Appel and Carlos Correa — to never play in the majors.
Aiken, 17, put together a prep career that was nothing short of dominant. In three seasons, he pitched 1602/3 innings and struck out 260 batters while compiling a 1.09 earned run average, according to
MaxPreps.com
.
With a mid-90s fastball, a strong curveball and a developing changeup, the 6-foot-4 Aiken is more major league ready than the typical high school pitcher, and he said he was looking forward to soon being a part of a World Series-winning Astros team.
In a conference call after his selection, Aiken described himself as a hard-throwing left-hander in the mold of David Price and Clayton Kershaw.
“Those are the two people who I model my game after,” Aiken said. “I try to do everything they do.”
Becoming the first high school pitcher since Taylor to be picked first was humbling for Aiken, he said, but he believes he earned the distinction, having sharpened his focus after a trip to Taiwan with the United States’ 18-and-under team.
“It’s a big honor,” he said. “I’ve worked hard enough, and I’ve done everything I could to put myself in that position.”
The Astros, in an unprecedented move, were picking at the top of the draft for the third consecutive year. Houston has been rebuilding aggressively for the last few seasons and had the luxury of drafting a long-term project like the young Aiken because its minor league system is stocked with major-league-ready prospects. Correa, the first pick in 2012, was also 17 when he was drafted, and he has rewarded the Astros’ faith with a strong start to his minor league career.
Now the Astros will try to persuade Aiken to sign rather than honor his commitment to pitch for U.C.L.A. next season. Major League Baseball has allotted $7.9 million for Aiken’s signing bonus, which is a far cry from the $1.55 million ($2.7 million when adjusted for inflation) that the Yankees gave Taylor in 1991.
Things continued to look up for high school pitchers Thursday when the Miami Marlins picked Tyler Kolek, a right-hander from Shepherd High School in Shepherd, Tex., at No. 2.
A 6-foot-5 18-year-old with a 100-mile-per-hour fastball, Kolek was considered among the best pitchers in the draft, but the selection came as a surprise because the Marlins passed on Carlos Rodon, a polished college left-hander who was born in Miami and has Cuban roots. Many thought the Marlins would love to pair Rodon with Jose Fernandez, a Cuban and the 2013 National League rookie of the year.
Rodon ended up going to the Chicago White Sox at No. 3.
The draft is in its sixth year in a prime-time format, with the first two rounds televised on MLB Network. It will continue with Rounds 3 through 10 on Friday and Rounds 11 through 40 on Saturday.

EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — For more than two decades, Izod Center played host to some of college basketball’s biggest games. The N.C.A.A. tournament regionals were held here 11 times, and the 1996 Final Four was, as well. But the tournament has not been back since 2007.
On Thursday night, the arena again featured two premier programs as No. 2
Duke
defeated Connecticut, 66-56, before a near-capacity crowd.
The Blue Devils (10-0) improved to 21-1 at Izod Center, including 10-0 in the N.C.A.A. tournament. They won despite setting season lows in points and field-goal percentage (37.5 percent), and committing a season-high 19 turnovers. The Blue Devils had been averaging 87.6 points a game and shooting 53.7 percent, which were the third-highest figures in Division I. They have won all of their games by at least 10 points.
Still, Coach Mike Krzyzewski said the Blue Devils had struggled a bit since defeating Wisconsin, 80-70, on Dec. 3. After that game, Duke did not play again until Monday night because the players had exams.
“During these 12 days, we weren’t able to practice as much,” Krzyzewski said. “You can tell that we’re still not there. When we played Wisconsin, we were completely there. We’re not going to play at that level every game, but we’re not at that spot right now.”
The freshman point guard Tyus Jones led Duke with 21 points, and the 6-foot-11 freshman center Jahlil Okafor, a top N.B.A. prospect, had 12 points and 8 rebounds. Amile Jefferson added 11 points and 13 rebounds, and another freshman, Justise Winslow, had 12 points and 5 rebounds.
The
UConn
senior Ryan Boatright, who Krzyzewski said was the best guard Duke had faced this season, led the Huskies with 22 points. Kentan Facey added 14 points and 9 rebounds. The Huskies missed 9 of 12 shots from 3-point range.
“Our halfcourt defense was very good,” Krzyzewski said.
UConn, the defending N.C.A.A. champion, fell to 4-4. With the all-American Shabazz Napier and the starters DeAndre Daniels and Niels Giffey gone, the Huskies have struggled. They lost three consecutive games, including a 1-point home defeat against Yale, before beating Coppin State, 106-85, at home on Sunday.
Trailing by 5 points at halftime on Thursday, UConn tied the score at 30-30 when Boatright made one of two free throws. The Blue Devils then went on a 15-2 run, but the Huskies recovered and cut the deficit to 62-56 on a 3-pointer from Boatright with 2 minutes 1 second remaining. Okafor was fouled on the next possession and missed both free throws, but Winslow grabbed the offensive rebound and made a layup to put Duke ahead by 8 points.
“We’ve just got to get better,” Boatright said. “In game-time, crunch-time situations, we’ve just got to get better.”
After scoring 40 points and making all 13 of his field-goal attempts against Coppin State, the 7-foot Huskies sophomore Amida Brimah committed a foul 12 seconds into the game and was replaced. He had another foul less than a minute after returning and played only one minute in the first half. Brimah had no points and one rebound and fouled out with 1:24 remaining.
For much of the game, UConn had two players defend Okafor, who is projected as the potential top pick in the
N.B.A. draft
.
On Monday night, when Okafor scored 25 points and had 20 rebounds against Elon, he became the sixth Duke player to record at least 20 points and 20 rebounds in a game.
“After the first couple possessions, I saw they were double teaming me fairly quickly,” Okafor said. “It was me being patient, not rushing, not feeling pressure or anything like that, just making the easy pass.”
Krzyzewski said: “Jah’s got to get accustomed, and he is, to all different kinds of defenses. I thought he showed great poise in the second half of when to go and when not to go.”

To the Editor:
“
Climate Efforts Falling Short, U.N. Panel Says
” (front page, April 13) correctly points out the dire nature of the situation that threatens the very future of our planet.
The article blamed “congressional opposition” for thwarting President Obama’s effort to adopt “aggressive climate policies.” While many environmentalists have serious concerns about how “aggressive” the president has really been in this area, what is absolutely clear is that it is not “congressional opposition” that is blocking progress.
It is the fierce opposition by one political party, the fossil-fuel-funded Republican Party.
Not only does the Republican Party oppose efforts to cut greenhouse gas emissions, but most of its members also reject the science describing the reality of climate change.
BERNIE SANDERS
Washington, April 14, 2014
The writer, an independent, is a United States senator from Vermont and a member of the environment and energy committees.
To the Editor:
In their April 9 Op-Ed article, “
Global Warming Scare Tactics
,” Ted Nordhaus and Michael Shellenberger, veteran apologists for nuclear power, trot out their treadworn and empirically unsupportable argument that poor messaging by the environmental movement on climate change and its failure to embrace nuclear power explains the growing gap between Republicans and Democrats on whether global warming is caused by humans.
Many environmentalists would welcome nuclear power if it ever becomes safe and economical. Current construction costs for new nuclear plants run approximately five times the cost per megawatt of wind, solar or natural gas.
Even before Fukushima, private insurance carriers — the ultimate arbiters of risk — ranked nuclear power plants so dangerous that they would not indemnify them. Thanks to industry lobbyists, the public now bears most of that burden, along with the ruinous costs of waste disposal which, despite its promises, the industry has yet to solve.
The opinion gap on climate change will not be bridged by crafty messaging from scientists or public advocates. It is the product of a $500 million propaganda campaign funded by the carbon titans to deceive the public about climate science.
ROBERT F. KENNEDY Jr.
New York, April 11, 2014
The writer is president of the Waterkeeper Alliance.

The European Club Cup is one of the more unusual team events because it turns the world’s best players into chess mercenaries.
That explains how the Azerbaijani team that won this year’s tournament, which ended last weekend in Bilbao, Spain, included only three Azerbaijanis and depended on stars from Bulgaria, England, the Netherlands, China and Ukraine to clinch the title.
The team — sponsored by the State Oil Company of the Azerbaijan Republic, and known as Socar — ran away with the title, winning every match. Socar’s victory was not a surprise. Second place went to G-Team Novy Bor from the Czech Republic, which was seeded fifth and whose only loss was to Socar. Three Czechs were on the Novy Bor roster, but the team included two players from Poland and two from India.
Taking third was Malachite, a Russian team that stayed closer to home in putting its team together. Five Malachite stars were from Russia; two were from ex-Soviet states, Latvia and Moldova; and one from Hungary, a former member of the Eastern bloc.

After
yesterday’s feature
on the American middle class’s (relative) decline, the big newsmaker over at The Upshot today is
new polling on four red-state Senate races
, which shows Mark Pryor, the Democratic incumbent, with a surprisingly large lead over Tom Cotton in Arkansas, and races in North Carolina, Louisiana and Kentucky all effectively in dead heats.
A number of conservatives have cast doubt on the sampling in the surveys — pointing out, for instance, that a surprisingly small percentage of respondents report voting for Mitt Romney in 2012, in states where he won some his largest percentages of the vote. At the very least, the Arkansas result does look like a bit of an outlier, given the numbers that
other polls have produced
, and there are other, more general factors — many of them enumerated by
The Upshot’s own Nate Cohn here
— that make the results less encouraging for Democrat than the topline numbers alone suggest.
But at the same time, as Cohn points out
in another post
, the Times polling is not exactly working with a deeply pro-Obama sample: The president is between 10 and 20 points underwater in every state surveyed. And presidential approval, while historically
more correlated to House outcomes than Senate ones
, is still a useful indicator of the size of the hill that the Democrats need to climb this fall. So the fact that incumbents like Pryor and Mary Landrieu and Kay Hagan are keeping it close against that backdrop is reasonably good news for their party — a sign, if nothing else, that the “all politics is presidential politics” dynamic Republicans are hoping for hasn’t yet fully taken hold.
The best reason to bet on the Democrats doing somewhat better than expected in these races, though, isn’t current polling (we’re too far out, still), and nor is it merely the general pattern in which savvy incumbent senators eke out re-election in races that the red-blue map suggests that they should lose. Rather, it’s the more specific phenomenon of a Republican Party that, in the age of Obama, has proven remarkably adept at squandering winnable Senate seats and underperforming in Senate races, with all sorts of candidates, in red and purple states alike.
In part, this has happened because of primary fights that have produced freakishly bad nominees, like Sharron Angle and Christine O’Donnell and Todd Akin. But it’s also happened in slow-motion, under-the-radar ways, sometimes with establishment candidates and sometimes with Tea Partiers, in races that are close and winnable and then just … slipped … away. That’s how Ken Buck ended up losing Colorado to Michael Bennet in 2010, for instance, and how Republicans lost North Dakota and Montana in 2012. But those are just the most conspicuous examples. As Ramesh Ponnuru
has pointed out
, the striking thing about the ’12 Senate races was just how
many
Republican candidates, many of them perfectly respectable nominees on paper, ran well behind the not-exactly-world-beating Mitt Romney:
Romney was not a drag on the Republican party. The Republican party was a drag on him … He did better than Connie Mack in Florida, George Allen in Virginia, Tommy Thompson in Wisconsin, Denny Rehberg in Montana, Jeff Flake in Arizona, Pete Hoekstra in Michigan, Deb Fischer in Nebraska, Rick Berg in North Dakota, Josh Mandel in Ohio, and of course Todd Akin in Missouri and Richard Mourdock in Indiana. LONDON —  In the drizzle outside Craven Cottage, the stadium that is home to Fulham, one of England’s oldest professional teams, the knots of fans who gathered during training sessions Thursday night for a shot at the autographs of their heroes had two men atop their lists.
One was James Rodríguez, Real Madrid’s Colombian midfielder, who was the top scorer at last summer’s World Cup in Brazil.
The other was a quiet, unassuming 50-year-old whose glory days as a player crested when many of the younger fans clustering at the stadium gate were barely out of their cradles. His name is Jurgen Klinsmann, and what brought him to Craven Cottage, along with Rodríguez, was the friendly match set for Friday between Colombia and the United States men’s national team, coached by Klinsmann.
For Klinsmann,
bringing the American team to London
is something of a homecoming. He is celebrated here, as few other foreign players have been,
for his years at Tottenham Hotspur
, where he played with success during a nomadic career that also took him to Stuttgart, Germany; Milan; Monaco; Munich; and Genoa, Italy.
In his three years as the United States coach, Klinsmann has sometimes been less popular among his team’s fans than among those who cheered him at Spurs.
He stirred controversy recently with remarks that some American soccer officials interpreted as disparaging of his own players and especially of the quality of play in Major League Soccer, at least compared with the top European leagues.
Meeting reporters on Thursday, Klinsmann avoided reigniting that debate and instead noted the ties that made Fulham a natural choice for an American team competing in England.
Other top English clubs have fielded American players — the United States team’s best player at last summer’s World Cup, Tim Howard, is the longtime starting goalkeeper at Everton, and defender Geoff Cameron is a regular at Stoke City — but none have had as many American players on their rosters as Fulham. That list includes the former national team players Carlos Bocanegra, Brian McBride, Kasey Keller and Clint Dempsey. The current Fulham squad includes Emerson Hyndman, a promising young American.
The club was even nicknamed Fulamerica at one point.
“It is a very special place for us,” Klinsmann said.
In soccer, friendly internationals can, at their worst, pack all the punch of a damp firecracker. But the London contest has the potential to defy the norm. A day before kickoff, the game was heading for a sellout, with 23,000 tickets sold, a record for an international at Fulham.
While many London-based Americans are expected, most of the tickets appear to have gone to Colombians based in London and elsewhere in northern Europe, to the point that Klinsmann and others in the American camp have said that they are approaching the match as a Colombia home game.
Klinsmann has billed the London game and another friendly, against Ireland in Dublin on Tuesday, as important steppingstones on the path to the next World Cup.

ATLANTA — Since April, André 3000 has been on the road, traveling from festival to festival with his old partner Big Boi to celebrate the 20th anniversary of their debut album as Outkast. And on Sept. 26, he’ll star, under his original name, André Benjamin, as Jimi Hendrix in
“Jimi: All Is by My Side,”
a biopic about the year just before Hendrix’s breakthrough, when he moved to London, underwent a style transformation and squared off against Eric Clapton.
Don’t let those things fool you. Over the eight years since the last Outkast project, the Prohibition-era film and album “Idlewild,” André 3000, now 39, has become, through some combination of happenstance and reluctance, one of the most reclusive figures in modern pop, verging on the chimerical.
Invisible but for his fingerprints, that is. For the better part of his career, André 3000 has been a pioneer, sometimes to his detriment. Outkast was a titan of Southern hip-hop when it was still being maligned by coastal rap purists. On the 2003 double album “Speakerboxxx/The Love Below,” which has been certified 11 times platinum, he effectively abandoned rapping altogether in favor of tender singing, long before melody had become hip-hop’s coin of the realm. His forays into fashion (
Benjamin Bixby
) and animated television (
“Class of 3000”)
would have made far more sense — and had a far bigger impact — a couple years down the line. In many ways, André 3000 anticipated the sound and shape of modern hip-hop ambition.
And yet here he is, on a quiet summer afternoon in his hometown, dressed in a hospital scrubs shirt, paint-splattered jeans and black wrestling shoes, talking for several hours before heading to the studio to work on a song he’s producing for Aretha Franklin’s coming album. In conversation, he’s open-eared, contemplative and un-self-conscious, a calm artist who betrays no doubt about the purity of his needs. And he’s a careful student of Hendrix, nailing his sing-songy accent (likening it to Snagglepuss) and even losing 20 pounds off his already slim frame for the part.
“I wanted André for the role, beyond the music, because of where he was psychologically — his curiosity about the world was a lot like Jimi,” said John Ridley, the film’s writer and director, who also wrote the screenplay for “12 Years a Slave.”
In the interview, excerpts from which are below, André 3000 spoke frankly about a tentative return to the spotlight that has at times been tumultuous — the loss of both of his parents, followed by early tour appearances that drew criticism and concern — as well as his bouts with self-doubt and his continuing attempts to redefine himself as an artist. “You do the world a better service,” he said, “by sticking to your guns.”

I thought, “What would Hendrix want people to know that’s not on YouTube?” He’s a god, he’s an idol. But he did that onstage. He was totally the opposite in real life.

Americans have serious misgivings about the prisoner swap that freed Sgt. Bowe Bergdahl from captivity in Afghanistan, and most disapprove of President Obama’s failure to inform Congress ahead of the exchange with the Taliban, according to two new national surveys.
In a CBS News poll released Tuesday morning, 45 percent disapprove of releasing five Taliban prisoners being held at Guantánamo Bay in a trade for Sergeant Bergdahl, who had been held prisoner by the Taliban since 2009; 37 percent approve.
Similarly, in a
poll released Monday
by the Pew Research Center and USA Today, 43 percent said it was the wrong thing for the Obama administration to exchange Taliban prisoners for Sergeant Bergdahl, and 34 percent said it was the right thing.
The White House has argued that the circumstances surrounding the opportunity to obtain Sergeant Bergdahl’s release gave Mr. Obama the authority to bypass a federal law requiring the Pentagon to inform Congress a month before the detainees were transferred. Nearly three-quarters of those surveyed by CBS News said Congress should have been notified by the president before he approved the deal.
The Pew/USA Today poll asked a slightly different question, but still a majority said Congress should be informed. Most of those surveyed (64 percent) agreed that “the president should be required to inform Congress in advance of decisions like these.” Just 30 percent said “the president should have the flexibility to make decisions like these without informing Congress in advance.”
According to the CBS News poll, 56 percent think Sergeant Bergdahl’s release came at too high a price for the United States. And among military veterans, 65 percent said the United States paid too high a price.
Some of these misgivings may be tied in with concerns about terrorism. Nearly half of those surveyed by CBS News (49 percent) said the prisoner exchange would heighten the threat of terrorism, while 40 percent said it would have no effect.
Both surveys showed that reactions to the deal for Sergeant Bergdahl’s release differ along partisan lines. Most Republicans disapprove of the deal, while Democrats have a positive opinion of the agreement. Most military veterans also disapprove of the prisoner exchange.
The CBS News poll was conducted on landlines and cellphones June 8 and 9 with 1,013 adults and has a margin of sampling error of plus or minus three percentage points. The Pew Research Center/USA Today poll was conducted on landlines and cellphones June 5 to June 8 with 1,004 adults and has a margin of sampling error of plus or minus four percentage points.

The premier event at the Fall North American Championships, which ended last Sunday in Providence, R.I., was the Reisinger Board-a-Match Teams.
The winners were Richie Schwartz of Aventura, Fla.; Allan Graves of St. Johnsbury, Vt.; Boye Brogeland and Espen Lindqvist from Norway; and Lotan Fisher and Ron Schwartz from Israel. They finished just over three boards ahead of Nick Nickell of New York City; Ralph Katz of Burr Ridge, Ill.; Bobby Levin of Henderson, Nev.; Steve Weinstein of Andes, N.Y., and Jeff Meckstroth and Eric Rodwell of Clearwater Beach, Fla. Third were Zia Mahmood of New York City, Alejandro Bianchedi and Agustin Madala from Argentina, and Norberto Bocchi and Giorgio Duboin from Italy.
In the six boards between the top two teams, Schwartz gained 4 points and Nickell 2. If those scores had been reversed, so would the finishing positions. The diagramed deal occurred during the final’s first session.
In the given auction, the three-spade response by Levin (North) was a so-called mixed raise. This would typically indicate four-card support and 7 to 9 points — just below a game-invitational raise. Weinstein (South) passed it out.
Brogeland (West) led his heart ace, and Lindqvist (East) played his four, using upside-down attitude signals. West continued with the heart king and the heart seven to his partner’s queen.
At this point, East understandably shifted to diamonds. Here, he would have done best to lead the ten. Since his partner held the eight, it would have been a surrounding play, negating the power of dummy’s nine. When East actually led the diamond seven (third-highest from an even number of cards), declarer would have escaped for down one if he had played low from his hand. However, South put up his jack.
West won with his ace and switched to a club. East took dummy’s nine with his ten and led the diamond queen. Now the defenders had to take three hearts, two diamonds and one club for down two.
At the other table, after Graves (South) opened one spade, Nickell (West) made a takeout double. This was an aggressive call opposite a passed partner and at unfavorable vulnerability, but it can pay to compete at board-a-match.
Richie Schwartz (North) responded three hearts, showing a mixed raise in spades; Katz (East) cue-bid three spades to indicate high-card values; and South applied the pressure by raising to four spades. After two passes, East rebid four no-trump, and West’s five-club call was passed out. (Later, Nickell felt that both he and his partner should have doubled four spades.)
North led the spade king. South overtook with his ace and imaginatively shifted to his singleton trump.
West, thinking that South was doing this with jack-doubleton and trying to give him a losing option, took North’s club king with dummy’s ace and cashed the club queen. Then, even though West played the diamonds for the loss of only one trick, he had to finish down one.
Plus 100 at both tables gave the Schwartz team the point on the board.

Argentina made a puzzling and potentially provocative move on Thursday in its landmark legal battle with New York hedge funds, which are suing the country over bonds that it defaulted on over 10 years ago.
Judge Thomas P. Griesa of the Federal District Court in Manhattan has ruled that Argentina cannot make payments on its main class of bondholders without also paying the hedge funds what they say they are owed.
But on Thursday, Argentina announced that it had deposited $539 million with the Bank of New York Mellon, for the purpose of paying its main bondholders. A payment is due on their bonds on June 30. Confusing matters, Argentina had recently said it was “impossible” to make that payment.
Argentina’s motivation for moving the money to Bank of New York Mellon, the trustee handling the bond payments was unclear. By taking a clear step toward paying the main bondholders, Argentina risks further provoking Judge Griesa. He called for a hearing on Friday morning.
“This is a brazen step in violation of the court’s orders and it warrants a swift and decisive response,” Robert A. Cohen of Dechert, which is representing NML Capital, a unit of Elliott Management, said in a letter to the court.
Argentina’s decision to make a deposit at the Bank of New York Mellon comes soon after it
said it would negotiate
with the hedge funds. Those talks are meant to happen under a “special master,” an independent lawyer that the court appointed on Monday. But after a meeting on Tuesday between lawyers from both sides, further negotiations have not taken place, according to two people briefed on the situation who were not authorized to discuss the matter publicly.
The Argentina case could open a new chapter in the vast international debt markets that countries tap to fund their deficits. Some bond market experts say a hedge fund victory could make it harder for economically stricken nations to lighten their debt loads by striking deals with creditors. But supporters of the hedge funds say credit markets function better when the rule of law is upheld.
The legal battle has gone for years, stoking ill will toward the hedge funds in Argentina. Its president, Cristina Fernández de Kirchner, has called the funds “vultures.” The fight appeared to enter a frantic end game earlier this month when the United States Supreme Court
declined to hear the case
.
Argentina almost certainly understands that, unless it settles with the hedge funds, the deposited $539 million will never get to its main bondholders.  Bank of New York Mellon is unlikely to pass on the money to the main bondholders. Judge Griesa’s ruling says that intermediary banks would be in contempt if they paid the main bondholders without paying the hedge funds. Bank of New York Mellon, for its part, recently said that it would “comply with any court order by which it is deemed bound.”
Argentina defaulted on nearly $100 billion of debt in 2001. In the following years, most bondholders exchanged their defaulted securities for new bonds that were worth substantially less than the original value of the bonds. Some bondholders, known as holdouts, wanted to be repaid in full and didn’t participate in the exchanges. Elliott Management, founded by Paul E. Singer, has spearheaded the holdouts’ efforts.
Argentina could in theory reverse course and decide to pay the holdouts, a move that might clear away an issue that has been weighing on the price of its bonds. The country’s struggling economy might get a boost from a settlement if it led to lower borrowing costs.
But Argentina’s most recent actions may instead be designed to confuse its opponents as it prepares a plan to defy the holdouts.
The country could in theory swap its main class of bonds into new securities that are issued out of Argentina, away from the New York jurisdiction. But Argentina may find it hard to make dollar payments on such bonds. The dollars would probably have to be routed through intermediary banks, which would still be subject to Judge Griesa’s order.
The case is being tried in America because the disputed bonds were issued under New York law.

Silicon Valley has been working on new ways to bolster the flow of capital to small businesses, one of the nation’s main engines of economic growth. Those efforts took another step forward on Wednesday, when Funding Circle, a so-called peer-to-peer lending network, announced that it had raised $65 million in new funding and appointed Robert K. Steel, the chief executive of Perella Weinberg, to its board.
Index Ventures, a venture capital firm, led the latest round of financing for Funding Circle.
Peer-to-peer networks aim to connect borrowers with individuals or institutions that have money to lend. In doing so, companies like Funding Circle hope to exploit shortcomings that they see in the banking system. With less red tape, peer-to-peer companies believe that they can make loans more quickly than traditional banks. And they contend that they can direct credit to borrowers that banks might neglect.
“The market opportunity is huge,” Sam Hodges, a co-founder of Funding Circle, said. “There is a desperate need among really high-quality small-business owners, who banks aren’t serving.”
Mr. Hodges declined to say what valuation the latest investment effectively places on Funding Circle. The new money, he said, won’t be used to make loans. Instead, it will help finance an expansion of Funding Circle’s operations.  “We continue to experience robust demand,” Mr. Hodges said.
Funding Circle was founded in 2010 in Britain and started operating in the United States last year after it acquired Endurance Lending Network, a small-business peer-to-peer lending company. Mr. Hodges declined to reveal Funding Circle’s revenue and income numbers.
Peer-to-peer lenders still only represent a small fraction of lending. Small-business loans at banks totaled $291 billion in the first quarter, according to data from the
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
.  In the second quarter alone,
JPMorgan Chase
made $1.9 billion of small-business loans. Funding Circle, by contrast, aims to have made $100 million of loans in the United States by the end of 2014.
Still, peer-to-peer lenders may find plenty of borrowers who have slipped through the cracks of the banking system.
Dara Kennedy, the founder of Ayla Beauty, which specializes in products for people with particularly sensitive skin, borrowed $50,000 from Funding Circle in the fall of 2013. She has used the money to help finance the setting up of a small store in San Francisco and to make changes to the company’s website.
“If I went to a bank, the loan size that they wanted to provide was much larger than I needed,” Ms. Kennedy said. The loan has to be repaid in three years and has an interest rate of 10 percent. Ms. Kennedy has personally guaranteed the loan and assets in Ayla Beauty also secure it. She got the loan in three weeks. “It was pretty fast and seamless,” Ms. Kennedy said.
The federal
Small Business Administration
guarantees loans as part of its efforts to bolster lending to small companies. But entrepreneurs sometimes say the process of getting a loan backstopped by the agency is lengthy. In addition, they may not qualify, especially if they don’t already have a business.
George Abdallah, who needed a loan to acquire a
Papa John’s
pizza franchise in Los Angeles, said the latter was the case with him. So he borrowed $70,000 from Funding Circle in January to help fund the franchise acquisition, paying 11 percent in interest over three years. “We’ve been doing great,” Mr. Abdallah said. “We haven’t even finished our first year and I am planning on opening a new branch.”
Small-business lending is not without risks. Businesses fail and lenders may not recover what they expected on defaulted loans. Funding Circle ranks its loans by the potential riskiness, giving them one of four grades. Its loans are evenly distributed across all four grades, Mr. Hodges said. Losses from defaults are running at around 1.6 percent of total loans, he added.
Since it was founded, Funding Circle has raised $123 million in equity funding, tapping investors that also include Accel Partners, Union Square Ventures and Ribbit Capital.
Funding Circle’s latest financing comes days after Social Finance, a peer-to-peer network that specializes in lending to students, packaged some of its loans into a bond and sold it to investors. The $251 million deal was a landmark for peer-to-peer lending because it carried a credit rating from
Standard & Poor’s
.
With interest rates at record lows, lenders may be attracted by the returns they can get on peer-to-peer loans. Mr. Hodges said that the lowest interest rate on Funding Circle loans is a little more than 9 percent. The company generates revenue for itself by charging lenders and borrowers fees.
One factor that will determine its success is whether the borrowers conclude that they are getting a good deal. Although Mr. Abdallah is considering using Funding Circle again, he would have preferred the loan he has now to have a longer term. “Three years was a bit short term,” he said. “Maybe they need to expand it to five.”
Madeline Willman, a spokeswoman for Funding Circle, said that the company had extended the terms of its loans to as much as five years.

A new show at the Philadelphia Museum of Art explores the work of the designer Patrick Kelly and his influence on Gerlan Jeans, a contemporary streetwear label. At left, a look from Patrick Kelly’s fall/winter 1987 collection; right, a look from the fall/winter 2009 collection of Gerlan Jeans.
The life and career of the designer Patrick Kelly were as brief as they were brilliant. A singular force in the 1980s fashion scene known for his jarringly bright and playful clothes, Kelly passed away on the first day of 1990 at 35 due to complications from AIDS. This weekend, the Philadelphia Museum of Art opens “
Patrick Kelly: Runway of Love
” (on view through November 30), the first retrospective of the designer’s prolific output since the Brooklyn Museum’s 2004
exhibition
of his works. The show brings together eighty complete looks from his ten collections produced between 1985 and 1990, gifted to the museum by the late designer’s partner in business and life, Bjorn Guil Amelan, and Amelan’s current partner, the choreographer Bill T. Jones.
A satellite exhibition, “
Gerlan Jeans Loves Patrick Kelly
,” traces Kelly’s legacy through the label
Gerlan Jeans
, founded in 2009 by the equally exuberant young streetwear designer Gerlan Marcel. Fifteen looks on display reflect the influence of Kelly’s bold graphics and uncompromising yet commerce-friendly whimsy. “I discovered Patrick through an article in Mao magazine while I was working for Jeremy Scott, designing graphics and prints,” Marcel recalls. “His journey from Mississipi to New York to Paris really resonated with me personally.” Marcel was born in London and raised in Ohio before finding her way to Paris Fashion Week and New York, where she now lives. “His energy and spirit came across so strongly, you could feel the emotion and the heart that went beyond the clothes,” she says of Kelly. “It was a whole attitude, a breath of fresh air from all the black-and-grey seriousness of so many brands and designers.”
“Patrick Kelly: Runway of Love” and “Gerlan Jeans Loves Patrick Kelly” are on view April 27 – November 30 at the Philadelphia Museum of Art, 2600 Benjamin Franklin Parkway, Philadelphia;
philamuseum.org
.

AUGUSTA, Ga. — Bubba Watson, the 2012 Masters champion, concedes his mind was not on golf last year.
“I was still celebrating my green jacket,” Watson told reporters on Friday. “How many green jackets you got? If you had one, you would celebrate it for a year or two.”
For more than 18 months, Watson disappeared in the green jacket, drinking in its charms and playing golf as if staggering from overindulgence.
“Never been drunk before,” he said. “But it was a hangover from the green jacket.”
Watson hit bottom at the end of the 2013 season when he finally looked past the green jacket and saw that he had fallen to 38th in the PGA Tour’s FedEx playoff standings. He was left off the 12-man United States team at the year-end President’s Cup competition.
“Those things hit you,” he said. “You ask yourself: ‘Are you going to dedicate yourself? Are you going to practice?’ It took time, but I knew I was ready to come back.”
For two days Watson has made a convincing case that his immoderation in the wake of a first major championship has ebbed. With five consecutive birdies on the back nine Friday — a streak during which he sank a 35-foot putt that broke 90 degrees and swatted a tee shot 186 yards with a 9-iron — Watson vaulted into the halfway lead with a four-under-par 68. Coupled with his 69 on Thursday, Watson had a three-stroke lead over the Australian John Senden and a four-stroke advantage over four others, including the defending champion Adam Scott, the 20-year-old Jordan Spieth, the Masters rookie Jonas Blixt and the journeyman Thomas Bjorn.
But the leader board also had an older pedigree. Fred Couples, 54 years old but ageless in the early rounds of the Masters, was tied for seventh at two-under par. It is the fifth successive year that Couples has been in the top 10 after two rounds.
Five other players 50 years or older also made the cut: Miguel Ángel Jiménez, Larry Mize, Vijay Singh, Sandy Lyle and Bernhard Langer.
There were some glaring omissions from the list of top contenders, which will leave the final weekend lacking in some star power. Phil Mickelson missed the cut for the first time in 17 years, completing his two rounds in 149 and five over par. With Tiger Woods out because of an injury, this weekend will mark the first time in 20 years that the final rounds of the Masters will be played without Mickelson or Woods.
Sergio García, Luke Donald, Charl Schwartzel and Ernie Els, who were at five over par, also missed the cut. Zach Johnson and Graeme McDowell finished at six over, Dustin Johnson was at seven over, and Ángel Cabrera, last year’s runner-up, posted a two-day total of eight over.
Swirling, gusty winds made for an unpredictable day that led to a bevy of quirky shots and outcomes. Rory McIlroy ended up in the azaleas when his approach shot appeared to strike a sprinkler head next to the 13th green and bounded in the air. McIlroy, who just made the cut at four over par, also flew his tee shot over the par-3 fourth green and over the adjacent fifth tee, ending up next to an out-of-bound fence.
Bill Haas, the first-round leader, who went from shooting a 68 on Thursday to a 78 on Friday, had to play a shot one-handed and backward because of a lie by a tree. Brandt Snedeker played a shot on his knees from heavy growth in the rough.
“It was pretty tough out there,” said García, who played with Watson. “Though not so much for Bubba.”

When García was asked if Watson’s streak of five birdies surprised him, he said: “Not really, because everything he had been doing before that was impressive. He just made a few more putts and was a little more impressive on those five holes.”
Watson’s birdie run began when he knocked his tee shot on the dicey par-3 12th hole to within 3 feet of the hole. His second shot on the par-5 13th hole left him about 14 feet for eagle. On the 14th, he had a curving downhill putt that was almost L-shaped, but it went in.
“I was lucky because Sergio chipped from behind me and his ball rolled right over my coin on the green,” Watson said. “So I knew where to hit it and how hard. Without Sergio’s chip, I probably would have three-putt.”
Watson’s chip on the 15th hole stopped about 4 feet from the hole, which made for an easy birdie. His titanic 9-iron to the 16th green nearly went in the hole for an ace.
His only glaring mistake was a bogey at the 18th when he missed a 4-foot putt. But it was just his second bogey of the tournament. Over all, Watson’s putting has been one of the most significant improvements in his game this season. It has come about, he said, primarily because of a new putter that is a half-inch longer than the one he had been using for years.
“It lets me have a more athletic putting stroke,” Watson said. “So after nine years of missing all of them, I’m starting to make a few.”
At the Masters, it also does not hurt that Watson is left-handed because lefties can fade the ball into Augusta National’s many left-to-right shaped holes. A fade is generally easier to control than a right-hander’s draw. Five of the last 11 Masters winners were left-handed golfers.
Watson was not disputing the theory on Friday, but in terms of his revival, he was more likely to focus on the changes in his personal life. Speaking of the last 18 months, he said, “I didn’t know how to handle it the best way, and so I didn’t play my best.”
As an example of the changes, this year he rented two houses — one for himself, his wife and young son and a second house for his extended family and friends. He has kept the distractions to a minimum and never tunes his TV to sports highlight shows.
“I’m learning how to be a champion,” Watson said. “I’ve learned how to practice the right way and how to focus my time on the golf course.”
Besides, there was one other major change in Watson’s life.
After one year, a Masters champion is required to give his green jacket back to the club.
But Watson would not mind putting it back on again soon.

Just this May, the Fire Department of New York posted training materials on its internal website detailing some of the difficulties encountered while battling blazes in homes brimming with hoarded belongings: blocked entryways, deep-seated fires and debris piled so high that, in smoke conditions, a “firefighter crawling atop can accidentally crawl out a window.”
The locations, known as Collyers’ mansions after the two brothers who died in their overstuffed home in 1947, present such dangers to firefighters that the department tries to keep track of them. As local fire companies become aware of hoarding conditions, a note is appended to the address in the Fire Department’s internal dispatching system so that arriving firefighters can be aware of what to expect.
The cluttered 19th-floor apartment where Lt. Gordon Matthew Ambelas died on Saturday night had not been identified as a Collyers’ mansion, fire officials said.
The department was still piecing together the circumstances surrounding his death, which the city medical examiner said Monday had been caused by a combination of smoke inhalation and burns. Investigators quickly homed in on the apartment’s crammed interior as a possible contributing factor, describing the home as presenting “Collyers’ conditions” in the hours after the fire.
“There was a lot of clutter in the apartment that impacted our operations,” said Francis X. Gribbon, the department’s chief spokesman.
The phrase refers back to the Harlem brownstone of Homer and Langley Collyer, brothers whose bodies were discovered in 1947 among 100 tons of hoarded belongings. No fire had taken place there, but the name came to define, for firefighters at least, the sort of pack-rat proclivities that are now recognized as a psychiatric disorder. As
much as 5 percent of the American population
may suffer from some degree of hoarding compulsion.
“Hoarding is a behavioral disorder that, in many cases, can go unnoticed, until other people are alerted to it,” said Zodet Negron, a spokeswoman for the New York City Housing Authority, which owns the building where Lieutenant Ambelas died.
Most of the time, such secrets are well concealed behind closed doors and city agents are rarely invited in. Periodically, they are revealed by fire.
When Collyers’ mansion conditions are known, a peculiar warning crackles across Fire Department radios in the midst of emergencies, an immediate indication that what appeared from the outside to be a simple fire is anything but.
But there is no formal list or tally. Nor does the city receive many complaints about hoarding.
More often than not, arriving firefighters only discover the teetering piles of belongings — the knickknacks and heirlooms that provide fuel for flames — as they burst through the door.
That was the case for the firefighters inside Apartment 19B of a Williamsburg high-rise on Saturday night. Flames and smoke overcame Lieutenant Ambelas, a 14-year veteran of the department, as he searched the packed apartment for possible victims.

Such blazes are “exponentially more dangerous,” said Daniel Sheridan, a battalion chief who works in the Bronx and has fought fires in Collyers’ mansion conditions from Chelsea to brownstone Brooklyn. “Outside was a beautiful brownstone,” he recalled of one fire location. “On the inside, you couldn’t get in the door.”
The recent training guide tells firefighters that such conditions may require alternate means of entering a burning home, including breaching the walls or using ladders to go through a window.
It also describes how to talk to New Yorkers who may live in such conditions before a fire ever starts. “Use respectful language,” it advises. “Don’t use words like ‘junk,’ ‘trash’ or even ‘hoarding’ as these words carry derogatory meanings.”
Firefighters are trained from the academy level up to deal with stuffed apartments, which complicate the search for victims and endanger the lives of those battling a blaze. Chief Sheridan recalled the death in 1999 of Capt. Vincent Fowler, who ran out of oxygen as he tried to make his way through the clogged basement of a Queens home.
James C. Hodgens, chief of the Fire Academy, said firefighters were trained to create a mental map of the space they were entering as they felt their way through what could be the pitch-black smoke of a fire.
“Just try to picture yourself going into a room where you can see nothing at all; you can feel around and get a sense of what type of room it is,” he said. “Now fill that room up with all types of objects. It’s difficult to know where you are.”
The fire commissioner, Daniel A. Nigro, was expected to attend the funeral on Thursday for Lieutenant Ambelas at the Church of St. Clare on Staten Island, where Lieutenant Ambelas lived with his wife, Nanette, and two young daughters.
Late Sunday, a message to her husband appeared on Ms. Ambelas’s Facebook page. “You were my everything and the rock of this family,” it read. “We will be together again until then I will raise our girls to make you proud.”

When I reviewed
the Cuban Crocodile
in Long Beach in 2012, it was the only Cuban restaurant I knew of on Long Island. It was damaged by Hurricane Sandy, and
Corazon de Cuba
opened in its former quarters less than four months ago.
There are at least a couple of other Cuban places on the Island now, but Corazon de Cuba beats out the competition. It is an attractive restaurant, too, though not particularly Cuban in atmosphere, except for its loud, pulsating Latin music (which will be lowered on request). The restaurant’s brick and stucco walls and dark wood tables set with cloth napkins and votive candles would be at home in an Italian or a New American spot.
The food, though, says Cuba loud and clear. Our favorite appetizer was the grilled steak bocadillos: bite-size pieces of extremely tender skirt steak that had been marinated overnight. Noe Dominguez, an owner, said in a telephone conversation after my visits that the marinade included “secret Cuban spices.”
Both Mr. Dominguez and his business partner, Armando Lopez, are originally from Mexico. Mr. Dominguez added that when he was a child his family vacationed in Cuba frequently, and it was then that he fell in love with the cuisine. The partners are first-time restaurateurs; their chef, Oscar Juarez, has cooked at Cuban restaurants in Manhattan.
Running a close second to the terrific bocadillos coming from Mr. Juarez’s kitchen was a seafood salad called Long Beach salpicon (the word means a medley or hodgepodge). The calamari, shrimp, scallops and mussels in the just-right lemon vinaigrette were distinguished by their freshness and the tenderness of the calamari. No chewy rubber bands here.
Also making a good showing was an avocado salad of lettuce tossed with red onion, tomato and green olives, all crowned with a sliced and fanned-out avocado half. Good, too, was a chicken empanada with thin, crisp, flaky pastry, an abundant filling and a tasty habanero-and-corn-cream on the side.
Two lesser lights were the shrimp fritters and a vegetable soup special full of broccoli, carrots, peppers and chunks of tender pork in a cream-touched broth; it needed a bit of salt to bring it to life. The fritters boasted a spicy tartar sauce, but they were boringly smooth and tasteless.
The best of three entrees highlighted in a box on the menu as Classic Cuban Dishes was the ropa vieja. This flavorful mix of shredded, tender skirt steak and onions, peppers and tomatoes arrived atop a mound of rice and surrounded by a necklace of tender but not mushy black beans. The ropa vieja was a better bet than the picadillo, a mixture of ground beef, potatoes, peppers, garlic, tomatoes, olives and raisins, which lacked flavor despite its numerous ingredients.
The third Classic Cuban Dish, shredded, slow-roasted pork, was succulent and fork-tender. That same delicious meat was the star of the traditional pressed Cuban sandwich, which also contained ham, Swiss cheese, pickles, mustard and mayonnaise in a large Cuban roll. An accompaniment of mariquitas (thin, crisply fried green plantains with a garlic-olive oil dipping sauce) made the dish even better.
All entrees arrive with rice and beans, including the fish of the day. The one we sampled was flavorful pan-seared cod atop crisp asparagus in a wine and garlic sauce dotted with cherry tomatoes. Paella Española, with shrimp, mussels, clams, chicken and chorizo enveloped in moist rice, was another crowd-pleaser.
Desserts are made at the restaurant. Only doughy banana fritters failed to please; we gave high marks to the moist and chocolaty brownie à la mode, the satiny flan and the flaky empanadas filled with rice pudding and served with ice cream and a strawberry sauce.
When asked, Mr. Dominguez said his favorite dish was the vaca frita, skirt steak that is simmered, marinated, then shredded and sautéed until crispy. I’ve got to go back to try it.

Jeff Kinney, author of the best-selling children’s series “Diary of a Wimpy Kid,” said Friday morning that he is opening a bookstore in his home town of Plainville, Mass.
Mr. Kinney spoke of his plans at a children’s author’s breakfast at Book Expo America, the annual publishing industry trade show being held in Manhattan this week.
The idea behind the bookstore, he told the audience, is to help restore the downtown area of Plainville, which is located southwest of Boston, near the Rhode Island border. He and his wife have moved slowly toward the decision, he said in a telephone interview Friday afternoon.
They purchased a centrally located building known as Falk’s Market that had fallen into disrepair about 3 years ago. Mr. Kinney said Falk Market used to be a “general store and a nerve center” for the area.
He has already torn down the structure and he said he hoped to replace it with a three-story colonial building that would house a bookstore, café, yoga studio and community center.
Mr. Kinney said the town did already have one used bookstore, but that the closest place to buy new books was a Barnes & Noble about 17 miles away.
The author, who has sold more than 120 million copies of the Wimpy Kid books, said that he understood that a bookstore was a somewhat risky financial investment.
“We know the margins are low and this is a tough business,'’ he said. “We expect to lose some money, but we are going to do everything to run a real and successful business.”
Bookstores are a passion of many authors, and other successful novelists have had a go at it, including Ann Patchett, w
ho owns Parnassus Books
in Nashville, and Larry McMurtry who owns Booked Up in Archer, Tex.

The governor of New Jersey is bullish on honesty.
“We are failing our taxpayers when we refuse to honestly address these problems and try to fool them into believing that choices do not need to be made,”
Chris Christie
said in his budget address in February. “We are better than that.”
The governor was talking at that point about public union pensions, a favorite whipping boy. If he had felt a seizure of honesty coming on, however, he might have done well to start barking the words “Pulaski Skyway” over and over again.
Because so much of what plagues his economically damaged state can be explained by the fate of that Neolithic-looking black iron and steel bridge that crawls over the Hackensack and Passaic Rivers. Each day tens of thousands of commuters beep and curse as their cars crawl across this ungainly bridge toward the Holland Tunnel.
Like a striking number of this state’s bridges and highways, the 82-year-old Skyway is on life support. This week state officials shut down its Manhattan-bound lanes for two years, while a billion-dollar repair is carried out.
Necessity is not the question here. The state transportation commissioner recently pointed to its rusting crossbeams and noted to The Record, a northern New Jersey newspaper, that the structure “is rotting away.”
How to fund these repairs, however, is a grave problem. The governor loves to talk of the New Jersey Miracle, but his state is a transportation pauper. Its transportation trust fund teeters on insolvency, with most of its money going to pay off old bonds.
Desperate to find funds, the governor embraced the chop shop option. First he killed a planned $8.7 billion commuter train tunnel under the Hudson River. Many argued this tunnel would ensure the future health of the region’s economy. Whatever: Today trumps tomorrow in politics.
Federal officials tried to renegotiate the cost of that tunnel, and the governor and his aides kept shaking their heads. “They could never take ‘yes’ for an answer,” a transportation planner familiar with these negotiations said. “They needed the money to fix their roads.”
Once Mr. Christie cashed in that Hudson tunnel, he demanded the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey allow him to use the unspent money for his bridges and roads. There was a rub, however. As The Record pointed out in
a fine article
a few weeks back, the Port Authority is not a transportation piggy bank. Its funds can only be used on roads leading to the George Washington Bridge and the Lincoln Tunnel.
The Pulaski bridge, alas, leads to the Holland Tunnel, which does not qualify, as it was built before the creation of the Port Authority.
The governor stomped and demanded. Soon the Port Authority’s lawyers rebranded the Pulaski Skyway an “access road” to the Lincoln Tunnel.
Legal fiction is a creative field.
The governor had other options. He could have sought to raise New Jersey’s gas tax, which is the second lowest in the nation. Every penny added to that tax is good for about $50 million. Raise the tax by a dime and you can repair a lot of bridges and roads.
Administered by a candid fellow like the governor, a tincture of persuasion and honesty might have helped residents understand that a tax increase would result in a $4 to $5 monthly increase for most drivers.

The average New Jersey driver now spends $600 each year fixing pothole-damaged cars. “It would have been a tough sell,” Janna Chernetz, of the Tri-State Transportation Campaign, said. “But you accept the governorship and you accept all the problems that come with it.”

Take it and offer no apologies. That approach at least has the virtue of honesty.

LONDON — Investors are doubling down on financial service start-ups.
Less than a week after Lending Club, an online peer-to-peer lender,
raised $870 million
through an initial public offering, Adyen — an Amsterdam-based payments processing company — announced $250 million in new fundraising on Tuesday that valued the company at $1.5 billion.
The new investment was led by General Atlantic, the private equity giant that also backed Facebook; Temasek, Singapore’s state-owned investment company; and the European venture firm Index Ventures.
And it is the latest foray by investors looking to profit from technology companies that are trying to revamp various parts of the financial services sector, which continues to struggle amid global financial uncertainty.
Adyen, which was founded in Amsterdam in 2006 and also has offices in San Francisco, acts as a middleman for companies like Facebook, Airbnb and Spotify to help them process payments in nearly 200 countries around the world.
To streamline how companies can process these payments, Adyen also has partnered with the world’s major credit cards and the likes of Apple Pay to create a single platform that now accepts almost 190 currencies worldwide. The company said that it expected to process roughly $25 billion in global payments this year, a 78 percent rise compared with 2013.
“Adyen is at the forefront of a rapidly globalizing payments market with tremendous growth potential,” Jonathan Korngold, global head of General Atlantic’s financial services unit, said in a statement.

WHEN politicians have trouble spinning their own glories, that’s a problem.
So it was bizarre that Hillary Rodham Clinton,
asked at a forum in April about her legacy at the State Department
, had trouble articulating it. That feeds into a narrative — awaiting her memoir on Tuesday — that she may have been glamorous as secretary of state but didn’t actually accomplish much.
In fact, that’s dead wrong, for Clinton achieved a great deal and left a hefty legacy — just not the traditional kind. She didn’t craft a coalition of allies, like James Baker, one of the most admired secretaries of state. She didn’t seal a landmark peace agreement, nor is there a recognizable “Hillary Clinton doctrine.”
No, her legacy is different.
For starters, Clinton recognized that our future will be more about Asia than Europe, and
she pushed hard to rebalance our relations
. She didn’t fully deliver on this “pivot” — generally she was more successful at shaping agendas than delivering on them — but the basic instinct to turn our ship of state to face our Pacific future was sound and overdue.
More fundamentally, Clinton vastly expanded the diplomatic agenda. Diplomats historically focused on “hard” issues, like trade or blowing up stuff, and so it may seem weird and “soft” to fret about women’s rights or economic development.
Yet Clinton understood that impact and leverage in 21st-century diplomacy often come by addressing poverty, the environment, education and family planning.
It’s not that Clinton was a softie. She was often more hawkish than the White House,
favoring the surge in Afghanistan
(a mistake, I believe) and
the arming of moderate Syrian rebel groups
(a good call, but one vetoed by President Obama).
Yet she grew truly animated when discussing the new diplomatic agenda. A couple of times I moderated panels during the United Nations General Assembly in which she talked passionately — and bewilderingly, for some of the audience — about civil society, women leaders and agricultural investments.
Pinstriped foreign and prime ministers looked on, happy to be considered important enough to be invited. They listened with increasingly furrowed brows, as if absorbing an alien language, as Clinton brightly spoke about topics such as “the business case for focusing on gender in agricultural development.”
Clinton was relentless about using the spotlight that accompanied her to highlight those who needed it more. At one global forum,
she went out of her way to praise Muhammad Yunus
, the Nobel Peace Prize-winning entrepreneur of microfinance, who was being persecuted by the Bangladesh prime minister. On trips, she found time to visit shelters for victims of human trafficking or aid groups doing groundbreaking work.
She may hide it, but Clinton is a policy nerd. Ask about microfinance, and she’ll talk your ear off. Mention early childhood interventions, and she will gush about obscure details of a home visitation experiment in Elmira, N.Y., that dramatically improved child outcomes.
The kidnapping of the Nigerian schoolgirls in April was the kind of issue Clinton was out front of. She understood that educating girls isn’t a frilly “soft” issue, but a way to transform a country to make it less hospitable to extremists. No one argued more presciently that women’s rights are security issues.

“Those who argue that her championing of outreach to women and girls and her elevation of development was not serious miss a central reality of international politics in this century,” notes Nicholas Burns, who was undersecretary of state in the George W. Bush presidency. “These issues are now mainstream globally.”
“I disagree very strongly with those who charge that Hillary Clinton was not successful,” adds Burns,
who is now at Harvard’s Kennedy School of Government
. “A fair-minded view is that she was, in fact, highly effective.”
Clinton was pioneering not only in the way she expanded the diplomatic agenda, but also in
the tools she forged to promote it
. She pushed government-to-people relations and people-to-people ties.
Some of this was pioneered in the George W. Bush administration, but Clinton greatly escalated public diplomacy with a rush into social media.
“She was very clear about it: This is the 21st century, and we’re fools if we don’t use it,” recalls
Michael McFaul
, who became ambassador to Russia in this time. McFaul then had no idea what a tweet was, and there was strong resistance from senior diplomats. “I said the boss wants to do this,” McFaul recalls, and he ultimately became a champion tweeter.
Today it’s routine to use social media in multiple languages to communicate American diplomatic messages to the world.
So, sure, critics are right that Hillary Rodham Clinton never achieved the kind of landmark peace agreement that would make the first sentence of her obituary. But give her credit: She expanded the diplomatic agenda and adopted new tools to promote it — a truly important legacy.
And, anyway, she may have grander dreams about how her obituary should begin.
